subject: How is Empirical Reliability being calculated

messages.author: 2d98f40c09e307a5
messages.subject: How is Empirical Reliability being calculated
parts:
I guess I don't understand how the empirical reliability returned by fscores is being calculated.  If I write a simple function that implements the definition of empirical reliability I find in the literature, I don't get the same number that is returned by fscores.

load(file="FRc.Rdata") # loading example data
FRcguess=c(rep(1/25,3),rep(1/20,2),1/25,1/15,1/25,1/9) # defining guess vector
m1.FRc=mirt(FRc[,-1],1,SE = T,guess=FRcguess) # estimate a single factor irt.  note the first column is stripped out because it is a student id

ER=function(fs){
  fs=as.data.frame(fs)
  out=1-mean(fs$SE_F1^2)/var(fs$F1)
  return(out)
}

> fscores(m1.FRc,returnER = T)
       F1 
0.6809699 

> ER(fscores(m1.FRc,full.scores=T,full.scores.SE = T))
[1] 0.5315063   #not the same number as returned by fscores

messages.author: 2d98f40c09e307a5
messages.subject: Re: How is Empirical Reliability being calculated
parts:
After spending some time in the literature following links in the blog.  I have come to the conclusion that both formulas are correct.  They however do represent different reliability coefficients.  The one I suggested is referred to by Adams(2005) as the person separation reliability, while the coefficient returned by the fscores function is referred to as the overall reliability coefficient.  If your interest is in assessing reliability in the estimation population level parameters, then the overall reliability would be the correct coefficient to use.  If your interest is focused on the difference between individuals, then the person separation reliability is the correct coefficient.  Thinking carefully about these coefficients is important.  If you use the wrong one (for your purposes) for bias correction, you could make things worse not better.

I have attached Adams 2005, because it was hard for me to track down.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: How is Empirical Reliability being calculated
parts:
Thanks for the pdf, Mark. I see what you are saying, but don't really understand the real purpose of the 'person separation' index. If one wants to compare individuals directly then you should do it directly, a la factor score estimates and their respective standard errors. No single composite is going to do better than the individual comparisons because it won't account for the respective variability of both response patterns (so a high person separation index might be very misleading in parts of the test where there is little information). 

My usual argument also applies to these indices: they are generally useless when missing data are involved (which happens a lot, and is where IRT is actually quite useful due to its FIML nature). An individual who answers 10 versus 30 items will have a much higher SE, and there the reliability composite will be deflated for the test as a whole (shrunken estimate towards 0 + a larger SE). IMO, it makes more sense to look at information functions to determine the ultimate utility of the test because it might work better for some participants than others, and is obtainable regardless of the observed response patterns. Cheers.

Phil

messages.author: 2d98f40c09e307a5
messages.subject: Re: How is Empirical Reliability being calculated
parts:
Thanks Phil,
My original post was brief so as not to bloat the blog.  Ultimately, we do intend to compare individuals via their scores (and other analyses).  But right now, we are in the instrument development phase. We are adding questions, rewriting questions, and deleting questions.  I will be using the person separation reliability as one of my metrics to monitor this process and keep the instrument moving towards greater informativeness.  To this end I was seeking a metric that reflected our ultimate goals, hence person separation reliability not overall test reliability.

Best MLT
